pep.name: Lex Greensill (Alexander David Greensill)
pep.position: Founder, person with significant control (owner) and former sole director of Greensill Capital (UK) Ltd. Former unremunerated external consultant to the UK Cabinet Office April 2012–2015 with a pass for direct access to Downing Street and a business card describing him as 'Senior Adviser in the Prime Minister's Office', later a Crown Representative — he has held UK public functions entrusted by government, making the company's owner a domestic-PEP-relevant person; his appointment and conduct were examined by the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee inquiry 'Propriety of governance in light of Greensill'

pep.name: David Cameron
pep.position: Former UK Prime Minister 2010–2016 — a politically exposed person by former senior public office. Special adviser to Greensill's board from August 2018 (part-time, ~25 days/year, paid a generous annual amount and held vested shares); he attended board meetings regularly but was NOT a director, PSC or owner of Greensill Capital (UK) Ltd — flagged as a PEP close associate of the entity

pep.name: Julie Bishop
pep.position: Former Australian Minister for Foreign Affairs 2013–2015 — a politically exposed person by former senior public office. Senior adviser to the Greensill board (member of its international advisory board and chair of its Asia-Pacific group, joined December 2019); NOT a director or owner of Greensill Capital (UK) Ltd

pep.name: Bill Crothers
pep.position: Greensill director (board member from August 2016) and former UK Government Chief Commercial Officer overseeing £40bn of annual government spending — a former senior UK civil servant, giving him a domestic-PEP profile as a director; he had also started advising Greensill two months before leaving the civil service in November 2015

pep.name: David Blunkett
pep.position: Former UK Home Secretary and Labour peer — a politically exposed person by former senior public office. Appointed to the 'expert advisory board' of Greensill's wage advance provider Earnd in November 2020; NOT a director or owner of Greensill Capital (UK) Ltd

pep.position: Former Metropolitan Police Commissioner (six years until 2017) — a politically exposed person by former senior public office. Paid consultant/adviser to Greensill's wage advance business Earnd from May 2020; NOT a director or owner of Greensill Capital (UK) Ltd

adverse_media.status: occurred; still ongoing — administration extended repeatedly, latest progress report filed 10 October 2026
adverse_media.summary: Greensill Capital (UK) Limited entered administration on 8 March 2021 after its main insurer stopped covering its receivables financing business; Chris Laverty, Will Stagg and Russell Simpson of Grant Thornton UK LLP were appointed joint administrators. The Greensill Group collapsed with combined liabilities of more than £1.6 billion, and unsecured claims against Greensill Capital (UK) are still estimated at about $1.6 billion.

adverse_media.status: reported; bank wound up, insolvency administrator appointed 16 March 2021
adverse_media.summary: BaFin suspended operations of the group's German banking subsidiary Greensill Bank AG citing an imminent risk of over-indebtedness, and filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors in Bremen after an audit found the bank could not provide evidence of receivables purchased from client GFG Alliance; a German court ordered the bank's wind-up and appointed an insolvency administrator on 16 March 2021.
adverse_media.category: regulatory enforcement — banking subsidiary wound up

adverse_media.summary: GFG Alliance, Greensill's largest client with roughly $5 billion of exposure, has been under criminal investigation in Britain since 2021 for suspected fraud and money laundering — an investigation that includes its financing arrangements with Greensill Capital (UK) Limited.

Zurich Insurance's defence and counterclaim (dated 26 January 2024) in a roughly $405 million London High Court battle alleges a 'fraudulent scheme' involving Lex Greensill, Greensill Capital (UK) Limited, Sanjeev Gupta and three Gupta Liberty businesses; Zurich alleges receivables sold by Liberty to GCUK were not genuine, that the receivables purchase agreement was a 'sham', and that Greensill made deliberate or reckless non-disclosures in breach of fair-presentation duties.

adverse_media.status: proceedings commenced (published 7 March 2024); May 2025 pause attempt and March 2026 strike-out application both unsuccessful
adverse_media.summary: The Insolvency Service commenced director disqualification proceedings against Alexander (Lex) Greensill for up to 15 years over his conduct as director of Greensill Capital (UK) Limited and Greensill Limited.

The UK Insolvency Service accused Lex Greensill of misconduct in dealings that led to $440 million of losses for a Credit Suisse investment fund and of making 'misrepresentations' in relation to Greensill Capital's insurance contracts; details emerged on 23 July 2024 after the High Court ordered partial release of the court document.

The administrators of Greensill Capital (the main UK company that collapsed into administration in March 2021) filed a lawsuit in London's High Court against founder Lex Greensill and six other former directors.
adverse_media.category: civil litigation — administrators' claim against former directors

adverse_media.status: trial began 5 June 2025; Lex Greensill named as key witness expected to give evidence
adverse_media.summary: Credit Suisse's (now UBS's) $440 million London lawsuit against SoftBank Group over Greensill-linked losses — alleging Greensill gave up rights to Katerra's debts in exchange for shares passed to a SoftBank entity, leaving the fund out of pocket on $440 million of notes — began trial; the collapse had already forced Credit Suisse to close $10 billion of Greensill-linked funds.
adverse_media.category: civil litigation — Credit Suisse/UBS v SoftBank over Greensill losses

adverse_media.status: settled on confidential terms; disclosed in administrators' April 2026 progress report
adverse_media.summary: The joint administrators struck a £71 million settlement with former auditor Saffery over its 2019 audit work; Greensill Capital's total insolvency bill has reached £83 million, among the most expensive UK insolvencies in recent history. Administrators continue to pursue claims against former directors and third parties, with proceedings linked to insurance coverage and regulatory investigations still live.

adverse_media.status: concluded — disqualification undertaking accepted 2 June 2026; nine-year ban effective 23 June 2026 until June 2035
adverse_media.summary: Lex Greensill, director of Greensill Capital (UK) Limited, was disqualified from acting as a UK company director for nine years after agreeing to a disqualification undertaking accepted by the Secretary of State for Business and Trade: in late 2020 he caused the companies to enter transactions with US construction company Katerra that removed legal protections from a Credit Suisse fund's investment without the required written consents, and caused or allowed Greensill Capital (UK) Limited to use $440 million received in November 2020 for purposes other than redeeming notes owed to the Credit Suisse (Lux) Supply Chain Finance Fund — the notes defaulted, causing a $440 million loss; his conduct breached the Companies Act 2006 duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence. A six-week trial due to begin 8 June 2026 was avoided by the undertaking.

output.risk_rationale: HIGH RISK. The subject entity, Greensill Capital (UK) Limited (Companies House 08126173), has been in administration since 8 March 2021 with combined group liabilities of more than £1.6 billion and unsecured claims still estimated at about $1.6 billion as of the administrators' April 2026 progress report; administration has been repeatedly extended (latest progress report filed 10 October 2026) and the insolvency bill has reached £83 million. Its controlling person and founder, Alexander David (Lex) Greensill (PSC since 6 April 2016, sole remaining director until his resignation on 17 June 2026, leaving zero current officers on the register), accepted a nine-year director disqualification undertaking effective 23 June 2026 after the Insolvency Service found he caused Katerra transactions that stripped legal protections from a Credit Suisse fund's investment and used $440 million received in November 2020 for purposes other than redeeming notes owed to that fund, causing a $440 million loss; the entity is also a named party in Zurich Insurance's High Court fraud ('sham' receivables scheme) allegations (from January 2024), was sued by its own administrators alongside six other former directors in May 2025, is tied to the SFO-era criminal investigation of client GFG Alliance, and its German banking subsidiary Greensill Bank AG was wound up by BaFin following a criminal complaint. No sanctions match was found on the OFAC SDN, UK OFSI consolidated or EU consolidated lists, and no PEP hits were returned for any owner or director (closest association: former UK foreign minister David Cameron was once an adviser to the group, but holds no ownership or director role in this entity); the LEI 2138004D9J9DZUANAI93 lapsed on 2025-03-28. The combination of live insolvency, a disqualified controlling person, ongoing fraud litigation and regulatory action against group companies, against a clean sanctions/PEP screen, supports a HIGH risk rating.
